paper_title: WorldCast: World-Consistent Character Video Generation with Large-Angle Camera Control

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Precise camera control is essential for cinematic character video generation, yet existing methods struggle to follow large-angle trajectories with combined rotation, translation, and radius variation from arbitrary initial azimuths. Such viewpoint changes also reveal character regions unseen in the initial frame, causing geometric distortions, appearance degradation, and identity drift. To systematically study these coupled challenges, we introduce CLACT, a large-scale Character-centric dataset and benchmark covering diverse Large-Angle Camera Trajectories, with accurate camera geometry and multi-view character observations for training and evaluation. We further propose WorldCast, a framework for world-consistent character video generation under diverse large-angle camera motions. Specifically, we back-project the initial frame into a 3D point cloud using estimated depth, align the point-cloud scale with the target camera trajectory, and render it along the trajectory to obtain explicit geometric guidance and coverage masks. To complement the incomplete character information, we introduce Geometry-Aligned Memory Attention (GAMA). Using relative camera poses estimated jointly from the initial frame and multi-view character anchors, we express anchor and target-view geometry in a common coordinate frame. GAMA uses this geometric alignment to guide the retrieval and injection of view-relevant character features during generation. Evaluations across diverse large-angle camera trajectories demonstrate accurate trajectory following while preserving character geometry, appearance, and identity.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Recent video diffusion models have achieved remarkable visual fidelity in textand imageconditioned video generation [1, 2]. For cinematic content creation, however, visual quality alone is insufficient: creators also require precise control over camera motion [3]. In character- *Equal Contribution. (a) Generated sequences along tilted circular and lemniscate camera trajectories. (b) Quantitative comparison of camera-control accuracy (ATE ), cross-view geometric consistency (MEt3R ), and image quality (IQ ). Each star denotes method; colors distinguish method categories, while star size indicates image quality. Both axes are reversed, such that methods with lower ATE and MEt3R appear toward the upper right. centric videos, camera motion can reveal subject from different viewpoints, establish spatial relationships, and direct visual attention. Realizing such shots therefore requires not only accurate trajectory following, but also consistent preservation of character geometry, appearance, and identity across substantial viewpoint changes [4]. Camera-controlled video generation has progressed from camera-pose and ray-based conditioning to explicit geometric guidance derived from 3D renderings [59]. Recent methods further explore joint appearance-depth modeling and more expressive camera representations to support complex camera motions [10, 11]. Meanwhile, multi-view generation and video re-rendering provide complementary means of improving cross-view consistency and synthesizing novel viewpoints [1215]. Despite this progress, accurate trajectory following and consistent character generation remain difficult under large viewpoint changes. Large-angle camera motion introduces two closely coupled challenges. First, trajectories involving substantial rotation together with translation, radius variation, and arbitrary initial azimuths place significantly stronger demands on camera control. Limited trajectory coverage or inaccurate geometric conditioning can result in under-rotation, incorrect translation, and drift from the requested path [16]. Second, the same viewpoint changes progressively expose character regions that are unobserved in the initial frame, leaving their geometry, appearance, and identity weakly constrained [17, 18]. These challenges are inherently linked: the target camera trajectory determines both the geometry that the generated video must follow and the previously unseen character content that must be synthesized at each viewpoint. Explicit geometric guidance can constrain the former, while multi-view character observations provide complementary evidence for the latter. Effectively combining them therefore requires relating both sources of information to the target viewpoints within shared geometric reference frame. Existing data remain insufficient for systematically studying and evaluating large-angle charactercentric camera control. Current camera-motion datasets provide limited coverage of complex trajectories involving substantial rotation, translation, radius variation, and diverse initial az-

sections.title: WorldCast
sections.content: imuths [14, 19]. Moreover, camera-motion sequences are not consistently paired with complementary views of the same character, limiting the joint study of trajectory accuracy and cross-view character consistency [18, 20]. To address these limitations, we construct CLACT, charactercentric dataset and benchmark designed for diverse large-angle camera motion. Its training corpus contains 50,000 camera-motion sequences rendered in Unreal Engine 5 and 30,000 Blenderrendered samples with multi-view character anchors, while the evaluation set covers 42 synthetic and real-world character scenes under multiple trajectory families. Together, these data support both training and systematic evaluation of trajectory accuracy, character consistency, and visual quality across diverse camera motions and substantial viewpoint changes. Building on this benchmark, we propose WorldCast, framework that couples scale-aligned geometric guidance with geometry-aligned multi-view character memory. We align the relative scale of initial-view depth and camera translation, then back-project the initial frame into 3D point cloud and render it along the target trajectory to obtain geometric guidance and coverage masks. To complement character information missing from the initial view, we introduce GeometryAligned Memory Attention (GAMA). Using camera poses jointly estimated from the initial frame and character anchors, GAMA aligns anchor and target-view geometry in shared coordinate frame, enabling geometry-aware retrieval of view-relevant character features and their injection into the video tokens. As shown in Fig. 1 , the framework improves camera-control accuracy and cross-view character consistency while maintaining competitive visual quality. Our contributions are threefold: We introduce CLACT, character-centric dataset and benchmark combining diverse largeangle camera trajectories and multi-view character observations to support training and evaluation of camera control and character consistency. We propose WorldCast, video generation framework that couples scale-aligned geometric guidance with multi-view character memory for accurate large-angle camera control and consistent character generation. We introduce Geometry-Aligned Memory Attention (GAMA), which aligns multi-view anchor geometry with the target camera trajectory in shared coordinate frame, enabling geometryaware retrieval and injection of view-relevant character features.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Camera-controllable video generation. Camera-controlled video generation incorporates explicit motion conditions into video diffusion models. MotionCtrl disentangles camera and object motion, while CameraCtrl introduces camera conditioning [5, 7]. CamCo and CamI2V incorporate camera geometry and epipolar constraints into cross-frame modeling [6, 21]. VD3D and AC3D extend camera conditioning to video diffusion transformers [22, 23], while UCPE unifies camera pose, intrinsics, distortion, and orientation in common representation [10]. DualCamCtrl couples RGB and depth generation to strengthen adherence to camera conditions [11]. For video rerendering, ReCamMaster, DepthDirector, and CameraAnything generate new camera trajectories while preserving source content and dynamics [14, 15, 24]. Geometry-aware and multi-view generation. Geometric representations and complementary observations provide spatial constraints for viewpoint synthesis. 3DiM, GeNVS, and CAT3D study novel-view synthesis from one or few observations [2527], while ViewCrafter, MVGenMaster, and SEVA leverage geometry or multiple input views to synthesize target viewpoints [12, 13, 17].

sections.title: WorldCast
sections.content: For camera-controlled video generation, RealCam-I2V, Uni3C, and GEN3C introduce explicit scene geometry or trajectory-aligned 3D guidance [8, 9, 19]. ConfCtrl improves robustness to unreliable projections [16], while Lyra 2.0 and WorldStereo further explore persistent geometry and geometry-constrained memory retrieval [28, 29]. Our work instead relates multi-view character-anchor geometry to the target trajectory, enabling view-relevant character evidence to guide generation. Identity-consistent video generation. Subject-conditioned video generation seeks to preserve appearance and identity across generated frames. VideoBooth and DreamVideo introduce subjectspecific conditioning [30, 31], while ConsisID and Magic-Me develop mechanisms for identity preservation [32, 33]. ConsID-Gen uses complementary views to improve cross-view consistency, and Gloria represents character appearance through content anchors [4, 18]. Virtually Being combines identity preservation across viewpoints with camera control through customization based on performance captures [34]. We jointly address character consistency and large-angle camera control through geometric guidance and view-aware retrieval from multi-view character memory.

sections.title: 3.5 Training Data Construction
sections.content: We construct an 80,000-sample character-centric training corpus, comprising 50,000 UE5 cameramotion sequences and 30,000 Blender-rendered samples with multi-view character anchors, as summarized in Fig. 3 . Both collections cover 99 characters and 33 environments. Using assets from Fab1, UE5 combines diverse scenes and character actions with arc, large-angle orbit, orbitand-dolly, and free-form camera paths. Using assets from Sketchfab2, our configurable Blender pipeline automates character placement, camera configuration, preview, and batch rendering across varied initial viewpoints, angular spans, translations, orbit radii, and indoor and outdoor scenes. Each sample provides reference video, initial RGB-D, camera intrinsics and extrinsics, rendered RGB guidance, coverage masks, and complementary front, back, and side observations for the geometric conditioning and character memory in Sec. 3.3 and Sec. 3.4 . Further construction details and trajectory examples are provided in Appendix .

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Implementation details. We train our framework in two stages based on Wan2.1-I2V-14B. Stage 1 combines 76,698 rendered SpatialVID sequences [42] with our 50,000 UE5 sequences for cameracontrol training. We update 𝑓geo, the pretrained patch embedding, backbone self-attention layers, and Plücker camera projection 𝑓cam, while freezing the remaining parameters. Stage 2 initializes from the Stage 1 checkpoint and trains GAMA on our 30,000 Blender samples with multi-view character anchors, optimizing only the memory-attention bank and anchor adapter. Both stages follow the flow-matching objective in Eq. (2) with their respective conditioning inputs. We use AdamW with constant learning rate of 104 and zero weight decay. Training uses 81-frame clips at 832 480 resolution. Stage 1 is trained for 5 epochs with batch size of 64, and Stage 2 for 8 epochs with batch size of 32. Evaluation benchmark. We evaluate on CLACT, comprising 42 character-centric scenes: 17 synthetic and 25 real-world cases. Each case is tested under six camera trajectories spanning largeangle orbits, translations, and combined motions, with different initial azimuths. The benchmark evaluates camera-control accuracy, cross-view character consistency, and visual quality under viewpoint changes. 1https://www.fab.com/listings/2e872a96-686e-4955-8256-82fa19904f92. 2https://sketchfab.com/.

Compared methods. We compare against three groups of methods. Direct camera-controlled video generation baselines include CamI2V [6], Uni3C [9], GEN3C [8], Lyra 2.0 [28], and DualCamCtrl [11]. We further compare with 3D-aware novel-view generation methods, including ViewCrafter [17] and MVGenMaster [13], as well as video re-rendering methods ReCamMaster [14], DepthDirector [24], and CameraAnything [15]. Evaluation metrics. We evaluate camera control using Absolute Trajectory Error (ATE), Relative Translation Error (RTE), and Relative Rotation Error (RRE) [43]. Character consistency is assessed using MEt3R for cross-view geometric consistency [44], ArcFace identity similarity [45], and CLIP and DINO similarities [46, 47]. We report subject consistency (Subj.) and image quality (IQ) to assess visual fidelity [48]. Detailed benchmark configurations, baseline evaluation protocols, and metric definitions are provided in Appendix .

sections.title: 4.2 Comparison with State-of-the-Art Methods
sections.content: Quantitative comparison. As shown in Table 1 , WorldCast achieves superior camera control and character consistency while maintaining competitive visual quality. The gains span trajectory accuracy, cross-view geometry, and identity and appearance preservation. Additional reference views yield limited or inconsistent improvements for ViewCrafter and MVGenMaster, reflecting the difficulty of reliably aligning sparse cross-view geometry under large viewpoint changes. In contrast, our framework combines trajectory-aligned geometric guidance with geometry-aligned character memory, enabling more reliable large-angle camera control and character preservation. Qualitative comparison. As shown in Fig. 4 , we evaluate challenging trajectory combining large-angle orbit with dolly motion. We compare against Uni3C and MVGenMaster. Uni3C exhibits severe character distortion under large viewpoint changes, particularly in facial regions.

sections.title: 4.3 Ablations
sections.content: Table 3 First-stage camera-control ablation. Effect of individual components. As shown in Table 2 , the full configuration achieves the best performance across all metrics. Removing GAMA substantially degrades both camera control and character consistency, confirming the importance of multi-view character memory. Without anchor geometry alignment, rotation error increases markedly while identity similarity remains relatively high, highlighting the importance of relating anchor observations to target viewpoints. Removing foreground masking also degrades camera control, character consistency, and visual quality, demonstrating the benefit of isolating character information from scene backgrounds. w/o UE5 data w/o Plücker conditioning Camera Control 4.295 2.113 0.156 0. 0.359 0.275 Full Stage 1 Variant RRE RTE ATE 0.031 0.100 1.

sections.title: WorldCast
sections.content: Effect of UE5 data and camera-ray conditioning. We further examine the contributions of UE5 training data and Plücker ray conditioning to camera control. These ablations are conducted on the first-stage model before GAMA adaptation. As shown in Table 3 , excluding the UE5 collection increases all three camera errors, demonstrating the benefit of large-angle training sequences. Removing Plücker conditioning also degrades camera accuracy, showing that explicit camera-ray information effectively complements the projected geometric guidance under large-angle camera motion. Effect of anchor count. As shown in Fig. 5 , increasing the number of character anchors from one to four improves cross-view geometry, identity preservation, and appearance similarity under large viewpoint changes. This indicates that complementary observations help recover character information missing from the initial view and provide richer cross-view evidence. The smaller gain from three to four anchors suggests diminishing returns as additional views contribute less new information. Additional discussions, supplementary experiments, and more qualitative visualizations are provided in Appendix .

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: Figure 5 Effect of the number of character anchors on character consistency. We presented CLACT, character-centric dataset and benchmark for large-angle camera-controlled video generation, together with WorldCast, framework that jointly improves trajectory accuracy and character preservation under substantial viewpoint changes. The key idea is to combine scale-aligned geometric guidance with Geometry-Aligned Memory Attention (GAMA), which aligns multi-view character observations with the target camera geometry and retrieves viewrelevant character features during generation. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world scenes demonstrate more accurate camera control and stronger preservation of character geometry, appearance, and identity, while maintaining competitive visual quality. Ablation studies further confirm the importance of large-angle training data, explicit camera-ray conditioning, geometric anchor alignment, and multi-view character memory. Future work will explore more flexible anchor acquisition, more complex dynamic scenes, and longer or interactive camera trajectories.

sections.title: AI Use Statement
sections.content: Generative AI tools were used to assist with language polishing, translation, and the revision of scientific writing, including improving clarity, grammar, and presentation. All AI-assisted content was reviewed and revised by the authors. Technical claims, mathematical formulations, experimental settings, citations, and implementation details were verified against the corresponding source materials and our implementation. Generative AI was not used to autonomously conduct experiments, determine experimental results, or make scientific conclusions. The authors take full responsibility for the final content of this work, including all text, claims, code, and artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

sections.title: Ethics Statement
sections.content: This work studies controllable character video generation and therefore has potential applications in visual-content creation as well as potential risks associated with synthetic human imagery. Our training benchmark is constructed primarily from controlled simulations using licensed or publicly available 3D character and environment assets. Any released real-world evaluation data will exclude personally identifiable private individuals and will follow the applicable data licenses and usage terms. Although our method is designed for research on camera control and character consistency, character-generation technology could be misused to create misleading or impersonating content. We therefore discourage the synthesis of deceptive depictions of real individuals without their knowledge or consent and will provide provenance and documentation for released benchmark assets and generated examples where applicable.

sections.title: Reproducibility Statement
sections.content: We provide the architectural design, conditioning formulation, training strategy, optimization settings, and evaluation protocol in the main paper and appendices. The supplementary material further documents the construction of the UE5 and Blender datasets, camera and depth alignment procedures, baseline input adaptations, evaluation metrics, and additional ablations. The benchmark generator exports camera intrinsics, camera-to-world poses, depth maps, multi-view character anchors, reference videos, point-cloud renders, and coverage masks. Upon publication, we plan to release the benchmark generation and evaluation code, pose-alignment and identityevaluation procedures, trajectory configurations, training and inference configurations, and the settings required to reproduce results with the released checkpoint.

sections.title: B Training Data Construction
sections.content: We construct two complementary training collections: UE5 sequences for large-angle cameracontrol learning and Blender samples with multi-view anchors for character-memory learning. Table B.1 summarizes their training roles and camera configurations, while Fig. B.1 shows their scale, asset statistics, and representative trajectory settings. Figure B.1 Training-data composition and camera configurations. (a) Sizes and training roles of the UE5 and Blender collections. (b) Character and environment counts shared by both collections, together with the number of UE5 character actions. (c) representative Blender batch containing 36 rotational, 20 translational, and 16 combined trajectories. (d) Angular-span configurations of the camera trajectories. B.1 UE5 Character-Centric Camera-Motion Data Scenes and character actions. We render 50,000 character-centric sequences using 99 character models, 33 environments, and 96 character actions. The environments span indoor and outdoor

sections.title: WorldCast
sections.content: settings, including city streets, shopping malls, cafes, offices, and rural scenes, while the actions include motions such as waving, dancing, and cheering. Each sequence contains single character, with the character, action, environment, and camera configuration varied across the collection. For each characterenvironment configuration, we additionally render front, back, left, and right views as complementary observations. Camera trajectories. We design four trajectory families: arcs spanning 3090, large-angle orbits spanning 90360, orbit-and-dolly paths combining 90360 sweeps with camera-distance variation, and free-form trajectories generated by B-spline interpolation between multiple keyframes. Both constantand variable-speed camera motions are included. The configurations of the UE5 and Blender collections are summarized in Table B.1 , and representative angular spans are shown in Fig. B.1 (d). B.2 Blender Data with Multi-View Character Anchors Asset preparation and scene placement. We generate 30,000 samples using an automated Blender pipeline with Cycles rendering. The assets include indoor and outdoor environments as well as static, rigged, and animated characters. The pipeline computes scene bounds, rescales characters, and evaluates candidate placements based on ground height, visibility, and clearance. Character placement and camera framing are adjusted to maintain ground contact and keep the subject within view. Orbit centers are derived from the placed character geometry, while camera radius and focal length are selected according to character size and scene constraints. Trajectory generation. Camera trajectories are parameterized by initial azimuth, angular span, orbit radius, and translation direction and distance. The pipeline supports 180360 orbits, partial orbits from different initial viewpoints, pure translations, combined rotationtranslation paths, and smooth radius variation. representative batch contains 36 rotational, 20 translational, and 16 combined paths, yielding 72 candidate trajectories per characterenvironment pair, as illustrated in Fig. B.1 (c). Multi-view anchors and geometric outputs. We render front, back, left, and right observations of each character as multi-view anchors, together with the reference video, initial RGB image, initial-view depth, and per-frame camera intrinsics and extrinsics. The initial RGB-D observation is back-projected into colored point cloud and rendered along the recorded trajectory to produce projected RGB guidance and masks indicating regions unsupported by the initial view. The initial

sections.title: WorldCast
sections.content: image and multi-view anchors are further processed by the camera-estimation and geometricalignment procedure in Sec. 3.4 to construct the geometry-aligned character memory. Preview and batch rendering. configurable web interface supports asset selection, camera adjustment, four-view preview, and batch rendering. The previews enable inspection of framing, occlusion, and ground contact before full-sequence rendering. Persistent Blender workers reuse loaded assets across tasks, while asset identifiers, camera parameters, and rendering settings are recorded for reproducibility.

sections.title: C Benchmark and Evaluation Details
sections.content: This section provides additional details of the evaluation benchmark, baseline input configurations, and metric protocol used in Sec. 4 . C.1 Benchmark Construction Evaluation scenes. The evaluation set contains 42 character-centric scenes, including 17 synthetic scenes rendered in UE5 and 25 collected from real-world imagery. The two subsets provide complementary evaluation settings: synthetic cases offer controlled character and scene configurations, while real-world cases assess generalization to natural images and diverse visual content. All evaluation cases are disjoint from the training collections. Camera trajectories. Each synthetic or real-world scene is evaluated under six prescribed camera trajectories covering large-angle orbits, pure translations, and combined rotationtranslation motions. These trajectories span substantial viewpoint changes and diverse initial azimuths, varying the character content observed in the initial view and enabling joint evaluation of trajectory adherence and character consistency as previously unseen regions become visible. Evaluation inputs. Each evaluation case provides an initial character image and prescribed camera trajectory. For methods that support or require multiple reference views, we additionally provide multi-view character observations. Our method takes the initial image together with the corresponding multi-view character anchors. All compared methods follow the same target trajectories, with camera parameters converted to their native representations when necessary. Generation resolution and sequence length follow the native settings of each method. C.2 Baseline Evaluation Protocol The compared methods span three generation paradigms. We adapt the benchmark inputs to their native formulations while preserving the prescribed target camera motion. Direct camera-controlled generation. Camera-controlled image-to-video methods are provided with the initial image and prescribed camera trajectory following their native input formats. Novel-view generation. For novel-view synthesis methods, we evaluate both their native singleimage setting and, where supported, multi-image setting with character anchors. For the latter, we follow each methods native multi-view formulation and provide the initial image together with the character anchors as reference views. Target views are then synthesized along the prescribed

sections.title: WorldCast
sections.content: camera trajectory. This setting allows us to separately examine the effect of additional reference observations when comparing with our multi-view character conditioning. Video re-rendering. Video re-rendering methods take source video rather than single initial image as input. We therefore construct static source video by repeating the initial image along the temporal dimension and apply the same prescribed camera trajectory. This setup isolates camera-induced changes from source-video motion and provides common static-input setting for comparison with image-conditioned methods. Generation settings. Each method is evaluated using the generation resolution and sequence length supported by its native implementation. All generated outputs are then evaluated using the same quantitative evaluation pipeline. C.3 Evaluation Metrics We evaluate each method along three complementary dimensions: camera-control accuracy, character consistency, and visual quality. Camera-control accuracy. We recover the camera trajectory of each generated video using Depth Anything 3 [51]. To remove the global coordinate-frame and scale ambiguity of monocular pose estimation, we align each predicted trajectory to its target trajectory using Sim(3) Umeyama transformation. Following standard trajectory-evaluation practice [43], we compute Absolute Trajectory Error (ATE), Relative Translation Error (RTE), and Relative Rotation Error (RRE). ATE measures the RMSE between aligned and target camera centers, while RTE and RRE measure the translational and rotational errors of consecutive relative poses, respectively. Lower values indicate better camera adherence. Character consistency. We use MEt3R [44] to measure cross-view geometric consistency using all generated frames together with the four observation anchors. We further evaluate identity and appearance consistency using ArcFace [45], CLIP [46], and DINO [47] similarities. To account for large viewpoint changes, for each generated frame, we select the observation anchor with the closest camera pose and compute its similarity to that anchor. The resulting similarities are averaged over all frames and videos. Higher ArcFace, CLIP, and DINO similarities indicate stronger consistency, while lower MEt3R indicates better geometric consistency. Visual quality. We additionally report subject consistency (Subj.) and image quality (IQ) following their default evaluation settings [48] to assess the overall visual fidelity of generated videos.

sections.content: This section provides additional experimental analyses and qualitative visualizations to further evaluate the proposed framework. D.1 Analysis of Geometry-Aligned Anchor Routing View-aware anchor routing. We analyze how the generated video features retrieve character information from different observations under 360 camera orbit. Geometry alignment enables faster learning of view-aware anchor retrieval and achieves higher routing accuracy after convergence. frame and multi-view character anchors. For each latent position, the star marks the expected anchor whose camera pose is closest to the target viewpoint, while the outlined cell denotes the observation receiving the strongest attention response. We observe agreement for 19 of the 21 latent positions. Moreover, as the camera moves around the character, the dominant attention response progressively shifts across anchors with different viewpoints, showing that the memory branch retrieves character information according to the evolving target camera geometry. Effect of anchor geometry alignment on routing. We further compare the learning dynamics with and without Anchor Geometry Alignment. As shown in Fig. D.2 , geometry alignment leads to faster improvement in routing accuracy during training and achieves higher final accuracy. This suggests that explicitly relating anchor viewpoints to the target camera geometry provides stronger geometric prior for learning view-aware memory retrieval. D.2 Additional Qualitative Results Comparison across diverse trajectories. Fig. D.3 Fig. D.7 present additional comparisons across diverse camera trajectories, including large-angle orbits, orbit-and-dolly motions, spiral and hyperbolic paths, as well as conventional camera motions. The examples also cover different initial azimuths, further evaluating camera control and character preservation under substantial viewpoint changes.
